explanations: withUsers locks the follower first and the followee second, so the order depends on the direction of the call. If user A follows B while B follows (or unfollows) A at the same moment, one call holds A and waits for B while the other holds B and waits for A. AsyncMutex has no timeout, so both promises wait forever, and every later follow/unfollow touching A or B queues behind them. Acquiring the two locks in a canonical order (for example sorted by user id) removes the cycle.

release() shifts the first waiter from the FIFO array and calls it, handing over the lock without ever setting locked to false. locked only becomes false when there are no waiters. Only one waiter is resumed, and order is first-in first-out, so the third waits.

The read-modify-write on counters is only safe if the existence check and the update happen under the same locks; checking first and locking later would let two identical requests both see "not following" and each add one. The store has no such rule, checking inside the lock is not faster, and Promise.all has no bearing on it.

forKey creates and stores a mutex on first use, and nothing ever removes entries from locks, so it keeps one mutex per distinct user for the life of the process. There is no delete on release, no expiry, and no fixed pool.
